item.title: The Two Kinds of Philosophers—And Why We Only Need One
item.description:
Philosophy

The Two Kinds of Philosophers—And Why We Only Need One

Personal Perspective: Of swallows and moles, growing up, and the future of philosophy

Posted August 7, 2026

Let me pre-emptively apologize for the anger a polemical essay of this kind will, no doubt, cause in some readers. For there is no polite way of stating my conviction that a large number of the philosophy profession have misapplied their intellect in pursuits that have tarnished the reputation of our field. But I assure you that I harbor no ill feelings of hatred for my fellow philosophers or the field that we all love. I only feel pity.

The Mole and the Swallow
Source: Image created with Chat-GPT/AI-generated

I shall thus not apologize for laying a finger in the wound of philosophy’s pitiful state.1

Two years ago, the philosopher and veteran of the blogosphere Eric Schwitzgebel published a lovely book titled The Weirdness of the World—a book aimed at the public to show the mind-bending and strange views that have made it into current debates in philosophy, celebrating “a philosophy that opens” the horizon of our minds. Outsiders of philosophy sometimes look with bewilderment at the weird things that go on in philosophy and come to the conclusion that anything goes. Schwitzgebel wants to affirm that conclusion. We should celebrate philosophy for its wild speculations.

As a fellow philosopher, my view of philosophy could hardly be more opposed to Schwitzgebel’s vision. I think an anything-goes attitude turns philosophy into a circus in pursuit of spectacle. Not a serious academic enterprise in search of truth. With such different views on what philosophy should be, it almost seems like two entirely different creatures roam the floors of the philosophy department.

In a review of Schwitzgebel’s book that surprisingly made it into Science, fellow naturalist philosopher Edouard Machery had this to say:

There are two kinds of philosophers: swallows and moles. Swallows love to soar and to entertain philosophical hypotheses at best loosely connected with empirical knowledge. Plato and Gottfried Leibniz are paradigmatic swallows. Moles, on the contrary, rummage through mundane facts about our world and aim at better understanding it. Aristotle, William James, and Hans Reichenbach are paradigmatic moles.

Machery is well-known for his usage of psychological methods to study philosophical intuitions—that have shown armchair theorizing of philosophers to be entirely unreliable—and so it won’t be surprising that he considers himself a mole. He notes that his own writing has been aimed at curtailing “the flights of fancy with which contemporary philosophers are enamored” and accordingly was largely critical in his review. He writes that “Schwitzgebel’s arguments often rely on a commonsensical, but questionable, understanding of key ideas” from science, leading to wild speculation, such as whether the United States of America is conscious.

Machery does not hold back on this point:

Schwitzgebel prides himself on painting awe-inducing philosophical possibilities that go against common sense and that we do not have compelling reasons to believe; they are, in his terminology, “wild.” But he never asks why we should care about what common sense finds plausible or bizarre. Common sense is a poor guide to truth, and it should play little role in serious philosophizing.

article continues after advertisement

Finally, Machery concludes his review with the somewhat barbed compliment that if you enjoyed reading “Philip Goff, then this book is definitely for you,” but warns the moles of the world that the book is not for them:

It is brilliant, thought-provoking, and very enjoyable. But card-carrying moles who want to see philosophy add its stone to the ever-growing edifice of knowledge might be left dissatisfied.

[I have criticized Goff’s speculative views on consciousness elsewhere.]

Even the title of Machery’s review is ambiguous. Describing Schwitzgebel as “audacious” could be read as a compliment for his boldness to go to new places, but also describes a kind of recklessness and a lack of proper respect. Swallows, unfortunately, show little respect for the intellectual achievements of science and even less for its actual outputs, being largely ignorant of what science has to say on the questions they are trying to answer.

Two days ago, I walked past a closed store which featured this cute little mole doll in its window. And it reminded me of Machery’s distinction between moles and swallows, prompting me to write about it. This morning, as I was finishing this post, I couldn’t stop myself from finding the store again and buying it. Moles got to stick together, after all. Treat her as a mascot for naturalist philosophy if you will.

While people often think of the history of philosophy as a long series of wild speculation that had little concern for empirical knowledge, that’s not quite right. Moles have always existed.

Aristotle, whom Machery identifies as a mole, spent much of his time observing the natural world and ended up writing some of the first systematization attempts of the living world, which made him the father of biology in the eyes of many—something we have unfortunately largely forgotten.

article continues after advertisement

Hans Reichenbach was an incredibly influential philosopher who published a book in 1951 titled The Rise of Scientific Philosophy, in which he argued that the scientific revolution finally allows us to leave behind the speculative philosophy of the past, which merely asks questions without ultimately answering them. Here is a lovely passage from it that nicely captures the spirit behind much of my recent criticisms of non-naturalistic philosophy:

Despite disagreements in the detail, I could hardly agree more with Reichenbach’s general vision for philosophy, which stands in stark contrast to that of Schwitzgebel.

Ironically, Reichenbach is my academic third great-grandparent (five generations back through academic supervisors), which I learned when I dug a bit through the history of my lineage.

item.title: Having Peter Pan on Staff Isn’t All Bad
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Having Peter Pan on Staff Isn’t All Bad

How to approach Gen Zers that look a little different than older generations.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Young adults today are advanced in some intelligences and behind in others. We must spot where they are.
  • Supervisors and counselors must capitalize on this generation's "magic" and reverse what's tragic.
  • We must turn our frustration into fascination with these young adults today.

In my recent book, The Future Begins With Z, I write about leading Generation Z in the workplace. They’re so different from older generations that they often present a challenge to their managers. I just wonder—what if our greatest challenge could become our greatest solution to future challenges?

I describe Gen Z teammates this way. Their population represents the “Peter Pan Paradox.” Do you remember Peter Pan? He soared into London (something no one else could do), sprinkled pixie dust over everything, and made magic happen. In short, he brought unique gifts with him. At the same time, Peter Pan wanted to stay in Neverland, where kids never have to grow up. This simple analogy describes a new reality at work:

  • The age of authority is decreasing. Young people enter their careers with some magic, armed with intuition, a vision of the future, and a sense of where culture is going.
  • The age of maturity is increasing. Young people seem to be taking longer to mature socially and emotionally, and often have no professional experience as they begin their careers.

I smiled as I read a post on social media where someone shared their observations about Gen Z. It was a tongue-in-cheek meme that said, “Gen Z will drink one medium caramel latte, not eat a single meal till 4 pm, verbally abuse a racist, crack a joke about their mental health and pick up a tear gas canister with their bare hands, but get nervous when they have to call to make a doctor’s appointment.”

Focus on the Magic

Something magic and tragic is happening at work with these youngest employees. Because of what Gen Z brings with them, leaders will need to listen more to them than they used to listen to rookies, and yet coach more than they used to coach to onboard them. I say, let’s focus on the “magic” they bring.

One example is how Gen Zers are helping older colleagues learn to utilize artificial intelligence (AI) at work. Yep, you read that correctly. In my focus groups with Gen Z employees, most of them told me they were teaching their older workplace peers how to use AI to get their tasks done. It's quite amazing—they have no positional authority and yet they don't need it.

It's Reverse Mentoring

Nearly all the Generation Z workers I talked with admitted to using AI tools at work, saying it was a catalyst for their careers. What they didn’t see coming was how much faster they caught on than their older colleagues. Many reported that AI is helping to bridge generational gaps at work, as I relay in my book.

Consider what this means. The newest, youngest, least experienced, and least expensive team members may accelerate the production of your entire team. When we focus on the “magic” side of their contribution, it becomes a game-changer, and it bonds generations. One manager, Mark Dixon, explained that the dynamic between older and younger generations was "so impactful" because of its "reciprocity." Younger staff are using their AI skills to "guide" others and "introduce new ways of working," while older generations respond by leveraging their industry knowledge to help Gen Z use the technology more effectively.

article continues after advertisement

I just received an email from my friend Colin Webb. He was hired by a traditional company right out of college, and although he brought new ideas with him, his supervisor was not open to his input. After a year, this young professional quit and became an entrepreneur. He just started his third company, and I am impressed. Avatar Robotics makes labor unlimited, allowing anyone to do manual work from anywhere in the world. He’s building a future where millions of humans direct billions of robots to provide resources and services worldwide. I watched him guide robots from 3,000 miles away. It’s dazzling to my brain.

The Bottom Line?

I am increasingly challenging our traditional view of mentoring. It no longer looks like it did in the past, when seasoned workers made an effort to teach younger colleagues. Now, it goes both ways. And the sooner staff over 45 years old can swallow their ego and become learners—not just teachers on the job—the sooner Peter Pan can apply his/her magic. If we can put up with the “pixie dust,” we might just find that having Peter Pan on staff is not all bad.

item.title: Does Parental Chaos Play a Role in Psychopathy?
item.description:
Psychopathy

Does Parental Chaos Play a Role in Psychopathy?

Perceived unpredictability may foster impulsivity and meanness in males.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • The triarchic model of psychopathy features meanness, boldness and inhibition.
  • Male research subjects who recalled childhood chaos were more callous and reckless.
  • This finding supports the notion that a form of psychopathy derives from an adverse environment.
Source: Art by K. Ramsland

I’ve written about two men from the same family who separately became serial killers, Danny and Larry Ranes. Larry, the youngest brother by a year and a half, killed five men over two months in 1964. Once caught, he confessed to them all. Eight years later, Danny raped and killed four women, three of them with a teenage accomplice. He insisted he was innocent but got convicted. Although Danny thought Larry exaggerated their father’s brutality, both recalled his unpredictable behavior, random abuse, arbitrary punishments, and paternal indifference. He abandoned the family when they were 9 and 10, leaving his wife to raise four kids (the other two were girls). In court, the oldest sister acknowledged that their early home life had been chaotic and lacking in moral guidance.

I have long believed that the father’s erratic behavior, coupled with the mother’s passivity, had influenced their sons’ later antisocial behavior. Larry developed a persona of callous indifference, coming across as a sociopath to a professor who interviewed him in prison. The same professor thought Danny wasn’t as bad, but his coercion of a teenage boy into rape and murder was highly manipulative and the crimes were more brutal and predatory than Larry’s string of robbery-homicides. Both brothers had been impulsive, Larry worse than Danny.

Recent research validated my sense of the influence of an unstable household on the development of criminality. By no means can we generalize from a single family’s circumstances or attribute cause and effect from one study, but the research adds a suggestive piece of the puzzle.

Instability and Secondary Psychopathy

Psychologist Virgil Zeigler-Hill and his colleagues found a significant degree of correlation between an unpredictable home life and the impulsivity and lack of empathy seen in kids at risk for developing psychopathy—especially for males. The lack of consistency seems to undermine their ability to form goals and develop prosocial commitments. In the Ranes case, both brothers dropped out of high school. Their marriages (two each) were short-lived, including the one each had with the same woman. (A prison psychologist told Danny's first wife that due to the chaos of his upbringing, he might not know how to love.) Both took risks with their crimes and showed indifference to the harm they caused.

Genetic factors influence the development of psychopathy, so it’s possible that the brothers inherited an antisocial predisposition. No brain scans or genetic workups were ever done on them. Since environmental factors can exacerbate the genetic factors, the chaotic household might still be important. In other words, brain abnormalities might yield a “born” or primary psychopath, but the environment might “make” a child prone to developing psychopathic traits. Some researchers call this secondary psychopathy. Kids adjust to the anxiety caused from adverse circumstances by becoming callous or impulsive. They can’t plan for long-term rewards because they can’t predict what’s coming next, and they struggle to manage their hostility.

article continues after advertisement

The researchers in this study used the triarchic model of psychopathy in order to measure the effect of both harsh circumstances and instability on each of the three dimensions. “Previous research has often treated both childhood adversity and psychopathy as broad, unitary constructs,” said Zeigler-Hill to Science Direct. “We wanted to distinguish between childhood harshness and unpredictability while examining three components of psychopathy: meanness, disinhibition, and boldness. This allowed us to ask which features of childhood environments were associated with which adult personality traits and whether those patterns differed between men and women.”

Data came from three groups (American and Israeli community members and American college students), yielding 4,873 subjects, about 60% of which were female. More than half received some form of compensation. Each participant completed the Perceived Childhood Harshness and Unpredictability Scale and the Triarchic Psychopathy Measure.

Perceived childhood unpredictability was positively associated with both meanness and disinhibition but not with boldness. Male participants who remembered highly erratic childhoods reported more incidents of being callous, exploitative, and reckless.

“The findings underscore the importance of treating psychopathy as multidimensional because meanness, disinhibition, and boldness showed different patterns of association with childhood conditions,” Zeigler-Hill said. “They also illustrate why a difficult childhood should not automatically be equated with an unpredictable one.” A stable home with few resources might have a more beneficial influence than a resource-rich but chaotic home.

article continues after advertisement

The researchers don’t conclude that unpredictability causes reactive psychopathy. They also acknowledge that the questionnaire about early memories didn’t include physical violence, which could make a difference in the findings.

The Element of Perception in Childhood Instability

I liked that this research focused on perceived childhood unpredictability, as children can process their environment in their own unique ways. Larry, the younger and physically smaller brother, seethed over the way their father used forced competitions to set him up to fail. Danny viewed the same contests as a way to establish his superiority. Their acquired sibling hostility lasted for decades beyond the father's departure.

We can't eliminate a genetic influence in this family, but with three of the four kids describing parental unpredictability and both boys acting out with extreme violence, I think this environmental association needs more attention.

item.title: Is It Language You’re Using, or Just Words?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Is It Language You’re Using, or Just Words?

How we can tell if animals use language, or if it's only us.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • The difference between words and language is important in animal research.
  • Errors, and creativity, are key to language use.
  • Three features can help distinguish between language and just words.

A flurry of admonishments erupts from two parents nearby, and I turn to see a small child half-naked and rising from a squat on the gravel path. Pull your pants up! they say, pull your shirt down! as the child tries to parse these two at once in his moment of need, and it reminds me of a class I teach where we talk about what counts as language, and what is just words.

In the 60s and 70s, when people rearing chimpanzees in their homes were setting out to prove that our differences were really just a matter of environment, a kind of territorial push-back arose from the behavior science community doing something similar, and definitions flew of what might be the various forms of intelligence. Many animals, of course, through the millennia, have understood human vocabularies. Bring those ewes around to me, shepherds have said to their dogs, or Go sit over there.

But these might be distilled simply to individual words, which really are just sounds, and not unique to us at all. EWE. SIT. That, basically, is what the blue jay on my patio is saying to whoever she’s dealing with. And actually, the shepherd I met in Ireland last summer was cutting to the chase by just using a whistle to put on a pretty good show for those of us gathered in the little observation booth beside his field.

Three Key Features

One vital feature that distinguishes language and just words, argue those invested in these matters, is rule-based grammar. When an ape named Kanzi reportedly distinguished, with his little toys, between Put the cup on the dog and Put the dog on the cup, ripples of excitement went through the community. You can see how doing that requires that Kanzi not simply distill DOG and CUP and then search around for what to do, but grasp a meaningful relationship between the two that is *conveyed by the words’ relative order.* In human language, the difference between Ben saw Miranda and Miranda saw Ben is deep and fundamental.

Another vital feature is what’s called generativity – producing new forms that you’ve never before heard, but that nonetheless make sense. An ape named Washoe once spontaneously signed with her hands, on seeing a zebra for the first time in a book, tiger-horse, and this is still so exciting to me that I tell every student in Intro to Psych about it every year. Human children do this all the time to solve language problems — I goed [went] to the park, We’ll do it nexterday [tomorrow] — and it's delightful.

English uses only about 44 sounds to make every word we say (the Taa language in southern Africa uses 100, the Hawaiian language uses 13). No matter how many basic sounds a language uses, recombining whole words yields infinite possibilities. We can recombine the same, quite limited set of sounds and words in our language to make, at the drop of a hat, a new sentence that no one’s ever said before.

A third feature is that the words — whether they be spoken, or signed, or sung — are arbitrarily assigned, that is, independent of the thing to which they refer. Nothing about a turkey, or a shovel, gives a clue about its name; that name is just a random sound assignment. Nothing about me looks like “Sarah” sounds, and I do not consistently resemble my friends with that same name in a way distinct from people with another name. Our usage of “s” as a plural marker is arbitrary, and of course other languages use other ways to mark a plural — for example, German uses “e” or “n”. Human languages do have occasional words we call onomatopoeia, in that they *do* sound or look like what they represent (boing, trickle), but these are very rare.

article continues after advertisement

Errors as Insight

In graduate school, a teacher told me of a four-year-old neighbor who, on seeing the teacher’s mini-pitchfork-like flatware for the first time, soberly noted that at her house they had forks, not threeks. This child, a new language user and not yet literate, mistakenly believed words to be non-arbitrary — that forks are so called because they have four tines, as they almost universally do, a detail noted by the child in the madly ambitious data collection and theory building that characterized her everyday. In this way language is special, not exactly like regular data collection. Adults don’t notice because we’ve so thoroughly internalized the arbitrariness.

Back by the gravel path, in a small garden area, another woman teaches her preschooler the names of plants, and there is a halting exchange about echinacea. The woman points it out, and the child says “here?” and the woman repeats it twice more, and both look confused. It would be interesting if the child is hearing “this is Eck in Asia”. She also says “BAH-sul”, rather than “BAY-zul”, though she has no British accent otherwise, and the child’s other parent arrives a moment later and says “oh! BAY-zul!” The child must weed through all this — in the case of echinacea, it will help once he can read. Receiving and producing language is a monumental task.

Language as Deeply Human

There are dogs with huge vocabularies: one border collie named Chaser understood a thousand spoken English words. And for sure other animals have a number of different sounds that they make: Lions use about ten to communicate among themselves, mockingbirds can make up to 200, most of which are mimicry of things they hear. Language, though, simultaneously rule-bound and infinitely flexible, is distinct, and may make us unique.

I once heard a student ask another to “cc” her on an email. Why do we even say that? asked the other. Because, the first one said, like there are now two other people seeing it – see/see. That is not correct, but also genius. We think *about* language all the time, and that in itself might be a fourth feature of what defines it – collect your examples, share them!

article continues after advertisement

-------

**I’m focusing on spoken languages, but there are fascinating ways that manual languages, like American Sign Language, also carry regional “accents” based on shape and motion. And as a natural human language, ASL (and the many others, like IPSL, JSL, etc) has the three features above.

item.title: Can AI Learn to Scaffold Group Work Like a Teacher Does?
item.description:
Education

Can AI Learn to Scaffold Group Work Like a Teacher Does?

CollaBot users wrote better essays — but not everyone loved the experience.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • CollaBot combines retrieval-based accuracy with generative AI's flexibility to support group work.
  • Students using CollaBot wrote significantly better essays than those using task scripts alone.
  • Some students found its scaffolding helpful, others found the time-tracking feature stressful.

Co-authored by Kodie Curran, Hannah Feeney, Jessica Murphy, and Michael Hogan.

Collaborative learning has been shown to promote greater academic achievement, more positive attitudes towards learning, and increased persistence in the classroom (Springer, 1999). However, orchestrating collaborative learning effectively remains a significant challenge for teachers (Dillenbourg, 2013).

It’s easier to lecture one group of silent students than to open Pandora’s box of collaborative learning. We all recognize the scenario: The teacher strives to give equal attention to each group working together in the classroom – yet one group struggles to move past the first task; another can’t agree on a shared focus; and another relies on a single student to carry the group’s workload. As the deadline approaches to present their results, the students are stressed, and the teacher is fatigued. These disruptions to collaborative learning — cognitive, socio-emotional, and participation challenges — are precisely what CollaBot, designed by Hu et al. (2025), was built to mitigate.

When conversational agents were first introduced to this process as a helping hand for teachers and students, they lacked personalization and flexibility. Being able only to retrieve pre-defined responses from a static knowledge base, they struggled to meet the varied, shifting needs of a live collaborative group. Then came generative AI, rich in flexibility, but prone to inaccurate, invented content. CollaBot operates on a retrieval-augmented generation system (RAG) that combines the benefits of these two AI system design architectures to give students information that is accurate and suited to their needs. CollaBot uses the RAG method to retrieve information from the educational knowledge domain, combines it with scaffolding strategies and the group’s ongoing work, and feeds this context into a large language model that works to provide students with its best possible response.

While many studies have explored the use of general-purpose conversational agents by individual learners, CollaBot is designed specifically for collaborative educational contexts. Pedagogical experts designed CollaBot to simulate Van de Pol’s Contingent Teaching Model, bringing the trusted diagnose-and-prescribe scaffolding approach from the real classroom to the virtual learning environment. A diagnosing module tunes into times of silence, uncertainty, and emotional difficulty by tracking writing and dialogic behaviours. When it detects a "critical event," a scaffolding module responds in one of three registers: cognitive, metacognitive, or social. Metacognitive and social support are triggered automatically and matched from a library of responses written in advance by pedagogical experts: When a group runs over time, CollaBot nudges it back on track; when members go quiet or grow frustrated, it offers encouragement. Cognitive scaffolding and support work differently — it arrives only when the students ask for it, and here CollaBot uses RAG to generate a hint or a fuller prompt, guiding the group without handing over the answer.

article continues after advertisement

From design to the classroom

CollaBot was trialed by an experimental group of thirty-nine undergraduate students, who were instructed to complete a collaborative writing task in seventy minutes on an open-source collaborative editing software embedded in the CollaBot learning environment. The task was completed in groups of three, who could request help from CollaBot directly or trigger it through a critical event. CollaBot operated from the group’s chat area, beside the shared space where students discussed and wrote. The control group completed the same writing task on a platform without CollaBot, which instead provided students with task scripts that guided them on the essay writing process. While other studies have compared groups using conversational agents to groups working without any support, this design provides a realistic comparison to existing classroom practices for group work. By doing so, we can investigate CollaBot’s effectiveness as a complement or extension of existing educational resources rather than a replacement for them.

The data collected from the students through pre-tests, post-tests, collaborative writing scores, and interviews showed that the experimental group achieved higher learning performance (69.77) than the control group (65.19) — a statistically significant difference. Writing quality accounted for 70% of that score, while 30% of the score was allocated to participation. Participation was measured by how much each student wrote, revised, and contributed to the group’s discussion. The significant effect of CollaBot on learning performance may reflect in part the metacognitive scaffolding feature available to the students, which encouraged individual participation and kept track of group productivity.

On self-efficacy for writing, the two groups showed no significant difference, yet both improved between the pre-test and post-test. This points to CollaBot and the task scripts being equally effective for building students’ confidence in collaborative writing tasks.

Better scores, mixed feelings

Feedback from the CollaBot group was mostly positive. Students credited it with improving their writing, with one student reporting they adopted its advanced "expressions and vocabulary." CollaBot also worked as a social buffer, with another student reporting "the chatbot helped us to break that silence and facilitated us to cooperate."

Although students reported some of CollaBot’s feedback as "ambiguous," this may reflect its deliberate use of hints designed to keep students thinking rather than hand over answers — the opposite of general-purpose GenAI systems designed to resolve a query and provide an answer as fast as possible.

The students had mixed experiences with CollaBot’s metacognitive scaffolding, with one commenting positively on "a better job in time allocation" and another expressing that the time-keeping feature led to "anxious" and "uneasy" feelings.

article continues after advertisement

The task itself was demanding. Writing a 200–350-word argumentative essay in seventy minutes is hard enough without also learning to work with an unfamiliar chatbot. In a normal classroom, where students already know one another and the tool, CollaBot’s benefits might be greater still.

CollaBot significantly outperformed the task scripts on learning performance and matched the benefits of the task scripts on students’ writing self-efficacy. But the more important finding from this study is that it demonstrates how technologies like CollaBot can be designed to simulate and enhance established teaching methods — and, unlike general-purpose GenAI, CollaBot was built with pedagogical intent from the start. As learning increasingly takes place in virtual classrooms, educational technologies should evolve to reflect this change without abandoning effective teaching practices. Students should have access to technologies that preserve the values of collaborative learning, especially in times of isolation due to illness or other life commitments. Rather than ask whether AI belongs in the classroom, shouldn’t we ask instead how it can best support the collaborative learning methods that already work?

Kodie Curran, Hannah Feeney, and Jessica Murphy are researchers working at the University of Galway.
